newsitem.title: USA: Albright endorses food aid for North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Albright endorses food aid for North Korea.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday endorsed U.S. food aid for North Korea to maintain stability in the Stalinist state.

"We...think that it is important to give some food assistance to North Korea through the World Food Programme because instability in North Korea is not to anybody's advantage," she told a congressional subcommittee.

The State Department said on Tuesday that World Food Programme has formally appealed for $41.6 million in new food aid for North Korea and officials said the United States was certain to make a contribution.

Albright did not say how much additional aid the United States might contribute but experts have said Washington was expected to donate at least $8.425 million; South Korea, about $3 million, and Japan, about $6 million -- roughly the same as last year.
U.S. officials have acknowledged that the World Food Programme, a U.N. agency, had limited its appeal to only a fraction of North Korea's needs, estimated at 2.3 million tons of foodstuffs.

They say it would be impossible for the programme to meet all of the Stalinist state's acute food needs, brought to a crisis by massive floods in 1995 and 1996. As a result, donations must be supplemented by commercial purchases by Pyongyang.

The United States has given Minneapolis-based grain giant Cargill Inc. a license to export 500,000 metric tons of foodstuffs to North Korea but Pyongyang and the company have been unable to strike a deal on financing.

Albright, who is to visit U.S. ally South Korea on an 11-day tour of major European and Asian capitals that begins on Saturday, said "we are very concerned ... about developments on the Korean peninsula."
She said she deliberately broke tradition by making her first overseas trip to Europe and Asia -- not just Europe -- to emphasise the importance of both regions to the United States.

She said Washington remains committed to a proposal advanced last year with Seoul for four-party talks that would include North Korea and China. The aim is to bring the rival Koreas into negotiations on a permanent peace treaty for the peninsula, divided since the 1950-53 Korean war.

North Korea was to attend a briefing on the proposal this month but has twice delayed the meeting because it wanted to complete negotiations on the Cargill deal. U.S. officials now say the briefing may not happen for a month or more.
